answers.answer: I would not add this cache now. Each receipt is read exactly once, so saving it after that read creates a copy that no later request will reuse. That first read still needs the database. The stated 4 ms database read fits comfortably within the 150 ms budget, and 15 reads per second is well below the stated comfortable capacity of 800. There is no demonstrated repeated work or database capacity problem for this cache to solve. It adds a cache write and another stored copy to manage, including its lifetime and updates if the receipt changes. Reconsider if many consumers or repeated polling start reading the same receipts frequently enough that reuse can reduce measured response time or database load. Measure hits and misses as well as before-and-after performance. If that changed workload requires every read to show the latest committed update, this lesson does not give a cache policy that guarantees that requirement: cache hits can be stale, invalidation can fail or race, TTL does not ensure fresh source data, and a shared cache is not automatically current. I would keep these reads tied to the authoritative database unless a freshness approach satisfying that requirement is established; the added freshness work can outweigh the benefit. The lesson does not teach a specific protocol guaranteeing latest-committed cache reads.

evidence.quote: First identify repeated work that is worth avoiding. A cache adds another copy to manage.
The entry is absent. The API reads the database, stores a copy in the cache, and returns the details.
Compare response time and database load before and after caching. Track the fraction of lookups that hit, and what happens during misses.
If requests rarely reuse results, or freshness is too hard to maintain, the cache may cost more than it saves.
A hit can still return an old price. Finding a value does not prove it matches the database.
These steps are not atomic. Removal can fail, or an overlapping read can put an older value back after removal.
TTL limits an entry's lifetime, not the age of the source data used to fill it.
Sharing reduces separate copies. It does not automatically keep the cache current with the database.
